title: @nytimes · 2026-09-19
text: President Trump abruptly announced a ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, even as it remained unclear how his prohibition would be enforced. What Trump’s ban would mean in practice was not clear and his aides did not immediately provide clarity. Journalists from those news outlets were working as usual on the White House grounds on Friday, and there were no signs of an imminent eviction. But the announcement was met with instant condemnation from many First Amendment groups, which called it unconstitutional. Read more about Trump's announcement at the link in our bio.

title: @nytimes · 2026-09-17
text: Jamie Beaton has 12 advanced degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oxford and other top universities, with more on the way. If he continues collecting advanced degrees at his pace, he will surpass Benjamin Bolger, who has racked up 16 at age 50. He might even beat Michael Nicholson, an octogenarian scholar with more than 30 degrees to his name. Aside from his studies, he is also the founder and the chief executive of a college admissions counseling service that has been valued at more than $600 million. His academic background has raised some questions, starting with: How can this be real? Is it education as performance art? An elaborate marketing ploy for his business? At the link in our bio, read our interview with Beaton and learn more about his path to collecting degree after degree. Photos by and via Jamie Beaton

text: This is the first issue of The New York Times, published 175 years ago. Then called The New-York Daily Times, it was printed on Sept. 18, 1851, by candlelight. To mark this anniversary, our journalists over the next three months will look back on the history and ideas chronicled in The Times — achievements and missteps included. Today, at the link in our bio or in our app, learn more about our reporter who was at the Battle at Gettysburg, take an in-depth look at what the journalism world looked like in the 1850s and play a special edition of an crossword. You can also comment “175,” and we’ll DM you a link to dive into our history.

title: @nytstyle · 2026-09-18
text: On and off the runway at New York Fashion Week, there was a conversation between sharper lines and slouchy silhouettes. There were subtle lessons in geometry. Deep V-necks that created stark triangular shapes; cutouts and keyholes that exposed precise peeks of skin; bold and buggy glasses that covered eyes. Asymmetrical pieces of fabric were layered onto other asymmetric pieces of fabric, creating shapes delightfully akimbo. These unconventional silhouettes found their way to the runways at shows like Michael Kors and Lii. Elsewhere, like at Coach and Eckhaus Latta, it was all about drape and slouch, with many designers gravitating toward silk and satin. These styles found their way to the streets too. Outside, some people were in slip dresses and camisole tops. Some, though, were eager to dust off their fall wardrobe, opting for heavier materials, like a leather skirt or oversize denim. Our photographer documented the street style at NYFW. Swipe through to see what people wore throughout the city and tap the link in our bio to see more photos.

title: @nytimes · 2026-09-17
text: Photojournalists captured images through the windows of Air Force One that showed President Trump reviewing a large poster board with what looked like a rendering of a construction site beneath three very visible words: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.” The Kennedy Center closed this week after a disastrous year and a half under Trump’s oversight that saw plummeting ticket sales and a talent exodus. The photos, which have been incorporated into a lawsuit over the fate of the institution, raise many questions that the White House has so far refused to answer. At the link in our bio, read more about the timeline.
